content: In both high and low HIV-burden settings, it is essential to offer HIV testing to all key populations and their partners across all healthcare services. This approach is an efficient and effective method to identify individuals living with HIV. Current guidelines recommend retesting at least annually for all individuals from key populations. Depending on individual risk behaviors, more frequent voluntary retesting may be offered. Mathematical modeling in Vietnam has demonstrated that retesting among key populations is cost-effective. Bi-annual testing may be considered in similar settings, prioritizing those at higher risk. Key populations, including individuals with chronic liver disease (such as those with hepatitis C), people living with HIV, sexual contacts of individuals with chronic HBV infection, healthcare workers, and others exposed to blood or potentially infectious body fluids, should be included in testing and prevention strategies. While the recommendation specifically includes people who inject drugs, this approach may also be appropriate for all key populations receiving HBV vaccination. Community-based HIV testing services linked to prevention, treatment, and care are recommended in addition to routine, facility-based HIV testing services in all settings. Trained lay providers can independently conduct safe and effective HIV testing using rapid diagnostic tests. HIV self-testing should also be offered as an approach to HIV testing services. Self-testing allows individuals to perform the test privately or under professional observation if desired. It must be voluntary, and individuals should not be coerced into testing or disclosing their results. Social network-based approaches can be offered as part of a comprehensive package of care and prevention for HIV testing among key populations. Provider-assisted referral should be offered to all individuals with HIV as part of a voluntary, comprehensive package of testing and care. For sex workers, the risks associated with disclosing an HIV diagnosis to clients or regular partners must be carefully considered, and disclosure should always be voluntary. Individuals experiencing intimate partner or other violence require assessment, support, documentation, treatment of injuries, and referral to appropriate services. Dual HIV/syphilis rapid diagnostic tests (RDTs) may be considered for use among key populations to increase access to both HIV and syphilis testing services. Further testing to confirm syphilis diagnosis or offer treatment depends on local epidemiology, past treatment history, available resources, confirmatory testing capacity, and national protocols. Mathematical modeling in Vietnam shows that using dual HIV/syphilis RDTs is cost-saving compared to separate tests at current coverage levels. Screening and diagnosing sexually transmitted infections (STIs) among key populations is a critical component of a comprehensive response to HIV and STIs. Periodic testing for asymptomatic urethral and rectal Neisseria gonorrhoeae and Chlamydia trachomatis infections using nucleic acid amplification tests (NAAT) is suggested for men who have sex with men and transgender and gender-diverse individuals. Periodic serological testing for asymptomatic syphilis infection is strongly recommended for these populations. WHO also suggests periodic screening for asymptomatic STIs, including chlamydia, gonorrhea, and syphilis, for sex workers. Self-collection of samples for Neisseria gonorrhoeae and Chlamydia trachomatis should be made available as an additional approach to deliver STI testing services. For individuals presenting with symptoms such as urethral discharge or anorectal discharge, management should be based on the results of quality-assured molecular assays. In settings with limited molecular testing or laboratory capacity, syndromic treatment is recommended to ensure same-day treatment. Similarly, for individuals with genital or anorectal ulcers, treatment should be based on molecular assay results. In resource-limited settings, syndromic treatment is recommended to ensure timely care. Hepatitis C virus (HCV) testing should be voluntary and not used to stigmatize populations at ongoing risk. Testing should be offered alongside evidence-based primary prevention services to reduce transmission risks and ensure access to appropriate treatment. To detect viremia, quantitative or qualitative nucleic acid testing (NAT) for HCV RNA or assays to detect HCV core antigen can be performed. WHO recommends offering treatment to all individuals diagnosed with HCV infection aged 12 years or older, regardless of disease stage. Pan-genotypic direct-acting antiviral (DAA) regimens are recommended for treating all adults, adolescents, and children aged three years and above with chronic HCV infection. For individuals living with HIV, antiretroviral therapy (ART) should be initiated regardless of WHO clinical stage or CD4 cell count. Successful ART with viral suppression prevents HIV transmission to sexual partners. People living with HIV should be systematically screened for tuberculosis (TB) at each healthcare visit. ART should be started as soon as possible within two weeks of initiating TB treatment, except when signs of meningitis are present. ART is also recommended for individuals with HIV and drug-resistant TB requiring second-line anti-TB drugs, initiated within the first eight weeks of anti-TB treatment. TB preventive treatment should be provided to individuals living with HIV who are unlikely to have active TB, including those on ART, pregnant women, and those previously treated for TB, even if TB infection testing is unavailable. Routine co-trimoxazole prophylaxis should be given to all individuals with HIV and active TB disease. STIs disproportionately affect key populations and should be diagnosed and treated promptly following WHO guidelines. Comprehensive guidance on managing symptomatic STIs, including gonorrhea, syphilis, chlamydia, and genital herpes, is available in WHO guidelines.
